You must produce:

2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions

• For related work and baselines:

  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.

• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The development of general-purpose pre-trained models for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is currently hindered by the rigidity of existing node representations. unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that generalize across tasks, GNN embeddings are typically "task-order specific." Embeddings optimized for low-order tasks (e.g., node classification, order-1) often fail or underperform when applied to higher-order tasks (e.g., link prediction, order-2) because different tasks require distinct, often conflicting, permutation symmetries. Current structural representations force a specific symmetry group during training, creating an "impossibility result" where a single static embedding cannot simultaneously be maximally expressive for tasks of different orders. This prevents the creation of a truly task-agnostic graph foundation model.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the limitation of task-order specificity can be overcome by decoupling the generation of node information from the enforcement of symmetries. We hypothesize that we can create "Holographic Node Representations" by splitting the embedding process into two distinct maps:
1.  **Expansion:** A heavy, pre-trainable map that generates high-dimensional, symmetry-free (positional) representations capable of distinguishing distinct views of the graph.
2.  **Reduction:** A lightweight, task-specific map that acts as a lens, re-introducing the necessary permutation symmetries to collapse the high-dimensional data into a task-appropriate embedding.

By treating node representations as a collection of diverse "views" rather than a single invariant vector, we believe we can pre-train a single model that allows for theoretically lossless adaptation to any downstream task order.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We plan to implement this concept through a architecture we tentatively call **HoloGNN**. The methodology focuses on a "pre-train once, adapt anywhere" workflow.

**1. The Expansion Map (Pre-training Phase)**
Instead of learning a single flat vector per node, we will generate a sequence of embeddings (a tensor) for each node. To ensure these embeddings capture maximal information and break the restrictive symmetries of standard GNNs, we will employ a **Symmetry Breaking** strategy.
*   We will utilize a standard message-passing backbone but run it multiple times in parallel or sequence.
*   In each run, we will perturb the features of a specific subset of "anchor" nodes (breaking their symmetry relative to the rest of the graph).
*   This process effectively creates multiple "views" of the graph. In each view, nodes that are usually structurally indistinguishable (isomorphic) will receive distinct representations based on their relationship to the perturbed anchors.
*   The output will be a stored bank of embeddings representing these multiple views.

**2. The Reduction Map (Adaptation Phase)**
When adapting to a specific downstream task (e.g., link prediction), we will not retrain the expansion map. Instead, we will initialize a lightweight, learnable aggregation module.
*   This module will query the stored expansion embeddings for the nodes involved in the task.
*   It will apply a set-aggregation function designed to enforce the specific invariance required by the task (e.g., ensuring that for a link prediction task between node A and node B, the representation is invariant to the swapping of A and B).
*   This map essentially "fuses" the distributed holographic information back into a coherent structural representation tailored to the specific task order.

## Expected Contribution
**Theoretical Value:**
We expect to formalize a representation framework that bypasses the known impossibility results regarding universal node embeddings. We aim to prove that this specific combination of symmetry-breaking expansion and symmetry-enforcing reduction is sufficient to distinguish isomorphic structures that standard message-passing GNNs cannot, effectively capturing spectral properties (like eigenvectors) without sign or basis ambiguities.

**Practical Value:**
This work will provide a blueprint for true Graph Foundation Models. By enabling a single pre-trained model to serve as the backbone for node, link, and subgraph-level tasks with minimal performance loss, we aim to drastically reduce the need for training specialized architectures for every new graph problem, facilitating efficient transfer learning in the graph domain.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We implemented a novel architecture (HoloGNN) designed to produce holographic node representations via an expansion map (symmetry breaking) and a reduction map (symmetry re-introduction). We evaluated the model's ability to generalize across tasks of different orders (node-level, link-level, higher-order) compared to various baselines.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Planetoid:** Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed (Citation networks). Splits: Standard splits for node classification; 85:5:10 edge split for link prediction.
    *   **MovieLens:** Multi-relational graph. Splits: 80:10:10 edge split for each task.
    *   **RelBench:** `rel-stack` dataset (Stack Exchange Q&A evolution). 38M+ nodes.
    *   **Synthetic Graphs:** Erdős-Rényi and Barabási-Albert graphs (for eigenvector approximation tasks).
    *   **OGB Molhiv:** Molecular graphs (for graph classification vs. link prediction transfer).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Planetoid:** Accuracy (Node Classification), AUROC (Link Prediction).
    *   **MovieLens:** RMSE (UserMovie task), Accuracy (MovieMovie, UserMovieUser, UserMovieMovie tasks).
    *   **RelBench:** MAP (Link Prediction / user-post-comment), AUROC (Node Classification / user-engagement & user-badge).
    *   **Molhiv:** ROC-AUC.
    *   **Eigenvector Task:** Test AUC (Link prediction based on eigenvectors), Runtime (seconds).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Standard GNNs:** SAGE (GraphSAGE), GCN (Graph Convolutional Network).
    *   **Task-Specific/High-Order Models:** SEAL (Subgraphs), NBFNet (Neural Bellman-Ford), NBFNet (no feat).
    *   **Positional Encoding Baselines:** SAGE/GCN + LapPE (Laplacian Positional Encodings).
    *   **Graph Transformer:** GPS (Graph Positional and Structural Encoder).
    *   **Spectral/Eigenvector Methods:** SignNet, Sign Equivariant Networks, MLP on eigenvectors.
    *   **Task-Agnostic Heuristics (RelBench):** Global Popularity, Past Visit, Random, Majority.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Framework:** PyTorch and PyTorch Geometric.
    *   **Hardware:** NVIDIA A100 and GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs.
    *   **HoloGNN Configuration:**
        *   Used **Parallel Breaking Algorithm** (except for eigenvector tasks which used Sequential).
        *   Used feature-marking for symmetry breaking (value 1 if broken, 0 otherwise).
        *   **Expansion Map ($T^*$):** 8 breakings (Planetoid/MovieLens), 10 breakings (RelBench), 2 breakings (Molhiv).
        *   **Structural Model ($f_\lambda$):**
            *   *HoloGNN (MP):* Simple message passing ($A^k(V_1 \oplus \mathbb{1}_v)$), $k=2$.
            *   *HoloGNN (GNN):* Shallow GNN (2 layers, hidden dim=input dim). Layer type varied by dataset (GCN for most, SAGE for UserMovieUser).
    *   **Training Specs:**
        *   **Optimizer:** Adam.
        *   **Planetoid:** 500 epochs. Hidden dim 64.
        *   **MovieLens:** Bipartite-SAGE backbone. 1000 epochs (HoloGNN/SAGE), 50 epochs (SEAL/NBFNet due to cost). Hidden dim 64. LR $\in \{0.01, 0.001\}$.
        *   **RelBench:** Mini-batch training (subgraph sampling). Gumbel-Softmax used for breaking node selection. 10 epochs (node tasks), 20 epochs (link tasks). Batch size 128.
    *   **Protocol:** Pre-train on a source task (of a specific order), freeze expansion map, adapt reduction map/head to target task (potentially different order).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Observation 1 (HoloGNN Stability):** We observed that HoloGNN maintained significantly more consistent performance when pre-trained on one task order and adapted to another, compared to baselines. Baselines often showed large performance drops (yellow vs blue bars in figures) when the pre-training task differed from the test task.
*   **Observation 2 (Specific Drop on Cora):** On the CORA dataset, adapting HoloGNN from Link Prediction to Node Classification resulted in a performance drop of less than 1.5%. In contrast, SAGE dropped by 7%, and NBFNet/SEAL dropped by 41%.
*   **Observation 3 (High-Order Task Adaptation):** On MovieLens, when pre-trained on the order-3 task (UserMovieUser) and adapted to other tasks, HoloGNN suffered a maximum drop of 9%, whereas SAGE suffered a 22% drop.
*   **Observation 4 (Scalability Limits of Baselines):** We observed that SEAL ran out of memory (OOM) on MovieLens order-3 tasks, and NBFNet was fundamentally incapable of handling order-3 tasks (marked NA). HoloGNN successfully handled these orders.
*   **Observation 5 (RelBench Generalization):** On RelBench, SAGE completely failed (0.0 MAP) when transferring from node-level tasks to link-level tasks. HoloGNN successfully transferred in this setting.
*   **Observation 6 (Eigenvector Quality):** Eigenvectors derived from the expansion map (HoloGNN) outperformed standard eigenvector baselines and "Sign Equivariant" networks on link prediction tasks, while being significantly faster than the latter.
*   **Observation 7 (Molhiv Transfer):** On Molhiv, adapting from Link Prediction to Graph Classification caused a 1.76% drop for HoloGNN, compared to a 5.77% drop for GCN.
*   **Observation 8 (Ablation on Breakings):** We found that small numbers of symmetry breakings (e.g., $T=4$ or $T=8$) were sufficient for obtaining transferable representations. Increasing $T$ to 64 yielded only marginal improvements.
*   **Observation 9 (GPS Comparison):** The GPS graph transformer suffered a dramatic 41.5% performance drop when adapting from Link Prediction to Node Classification on CORA, whereas HoloGNN dropped only ~1%.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The development of general-purpose pre-trained Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is currently hindered by the lack of suitable generalist node representations. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) which generate versatile embeddings adaptable to various downstream tasks, current GNN embeddings are inherently specialized to specific "task orders."

A task order is defined by the size of the set of nodes involved in a prediction (e.g., node classification is order-1; link prediction is order-2). Existing architectures produce embeddings that respect specific permutation symmetries required for a single task order. Consequently, an embedding optimized for node classification is often structurally incapable of distinguishing non-isomorphic links in a link prediction task, and vice-versa. It is mathematically impossible for a single "flat" structural embedding $f(A, X) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ to be most-expressive for tasks of different orders simultaneously. This limitation prevents the creation of a truly task-agnostic pre-trained graph model.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Holographic Node Representations**, a new blueprint for node embeddings capable of solving tasks of any order ($r=1, 2, \dots$).

Our core hypothesis is that we can decouple the storage of structural information from the enforcement of permutation symmetries. We hypothesize that by generating a high-dimensional, symmetry-free representation (the **Expansion Map**) that captures multiple "views" of the graph, we can encode sufficient information to distinguish isomorphic nodes. Subsequently, we can employ a lightweight, learnable **Reduction Map** to reintroduce the specific permutation symmetries required for a target task order at inference time. This will allow a single pre-trained model to be adapted efficiently to any graph task (node, link, or higher-order) without retraining the core feature extractor.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework called **HoloGNN**. The architecture consists of two primary learnable components: an Expansion Map $E_\theta$ and a Reduction Map $R_\psi$.

### 1. Initialization and Breaking Selectors
Let $G = (\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{X})$ be a graph with adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and node features $\mathbf{X}$. We will first compute an initial structural representation:
$$ V _ { 1 } = g _ { \mathrm { s t r u c } } ( \mathbf { A } , \mathbf { X } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d _ { 1 } } $$
where $g_{\mathrm{struc}}$ is a standard structural GNN (e.g., GCN or SAGE).

To drive the expansion map, we will define **Node-Breaking Selectors**, denoted as a sequence of functions $( h _ { \lambda } ) _ { \lambda = 1 } ^ { L }$. Each selector $h_\lambda(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{V}_1)$ will deterministically return a list of nodes $( v _ { \lambda , 1 } , \dots , v _ { \lambda , k _ { \lambda } } )$ that share a specific structural role (e.g., all nodes with the same degree), sorted by ID to ensure reproducibility. These selectors determine which nodes will be used to "break" symmetries.

### 2. The Expansion Map ($E_\theta$)
The expansion map will produce a sequence of embeddings by iteratively perturbing the features of selected breaking nodes. We will define the Expansion Map as:
$$ E _ { \theta } : \{ 0 , 1 \} ^ { n \times n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d _ { 1 } } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times T \times d _ { e } } \times ( 2 ^ { [ n ] } ) ^ { L } \times \mathbb { N } ^ { T } $$
This map outputs:
1.  A tensor of node representations $V(\mathbf{A}, V_1) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times T \times d_e}$ where $T$ is the number of views/breakings.
2.  The lists of breaking node IDs from the selectors.
3.  A partition sequence $\Lambda \in \mathbb{N}^T$ indicating which selector $h_\lambda$ generated which step $t$.

We will implement two algorithms for this map. The primary scalable method will be **Parallel Breaking**.

**Parallel Breaking Algorithm:**
For each step $t$, corresponding to a breaking node $v$ selected by $h_\lambda$, we will compute embeddings $V_t$ using a structural model $f_\lambda$. The input will be the adjacency matrix and the initial embeddings $V_1$ perturbed by a unique identifier (one-hot vector) for the breaking node $v$:
$$ V _ { t } = f _ { \lambda } ( \mathbf { A } , V _ { 1 } \oplus \mathbb { 1 } _ { v } ) $$
where $\oplus$ denotes concatenation. Crucially, because $f_\lambda$ does not depend on previous steps $V_{t-1}$, all $T$ embeddings can be computed in parallel.

The final expansion output is the concatenation of these views: $\text{Concat}(V_T, \dots, V_1)$ along a new dimension.

### 3. The Reduction Map ($R_\psi$)
The reduction map will take the symmetry-free output of the expansion map and fuse the $T$ views to produce structural representations of a specific order $r$ (where $r=1$ for node tasks, $r=2$ for link tasks).

We define the reduction map $R_\psi$ to act on a set of $r$ nodes $\{ v_1, \dots, v_r \}$. The process involves two learnable set functions, $\phi_\lambda$ and $\rho_\lambda$:

1.  **Within-step Aggregation:** First, we compute an intermediate representation $U_{\lambda, t}$ for the target set of nodes at step $t$:
    $$ U _ { \lambda , t } = \phi _ { \lambda } \Bigl ( \bigl \{ V _ { t , u } \bigr \} _ { \forall u \in \{ v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { r } \} } \Bigr ) $$
    This ensures the representation is invariant to the ordering of the query nodes (e.g., $(u, v)$ vs $(v, u)$).

2.  **Across-step Aggregation:** Next, we aggregate these intermediate representations across all time steps $t$ that were generated by the same breaking selector (indicated by $\Lambda_t = \lambda$):
    $$ U _ { \lambda , \{ v _ { 1 } , \dots , v _ { r } \} } = \rho _ { \lambda } \Bigl ( \bigl \{ U _ { \lambda , t } \bigr \} _ { \forall t \in [ T ] \mathrm { ~ s . t . ~ } \Lambda _ { t } = \lambda } \Bigr ) $$

The final representation for the set $\{ v_1, \dots, v_r \}$ is the concatenation of these aggregated features for all selectors $\lambda \in [L]$:
$$ R ( E ( \mathbf { A } , V _ { 1 } ) ) _ { \{ v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { r } \} } = \Bigl ( U _ { \lambda , \{ v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { r } \} } \Bigr ) _ { \lambda \in [ L ] } $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Pre-training Framework:** We expect to demonstrate that Holographic Node Representations allow for pre-training on a task of one order (e.g., link prediction) and adapting to a task of a different order (e.g., node classification) with minimal performance loss, solving the impossibility result of flat embeddings.
2.  **Theoretical Expressivity:** We aim to prove that our single-node symmetry breaking approach is sufficient to distinguish any isomorphic nodes that have different neighborhoods. Furthermore, we will show that specific instantiations of our Sequential Breaking algorithm can express canonical eigenvectors without sign or basis ambiguity.
3.  **Maximally Expressive Structural Representations:** We will theoretically derive that the combination of our Parallel Breaking expansion map and the proposed Reduction map produces representations that are most-expressive for structural tasks of order $r$, provided the breaking selectors are chosen appropriately.

preinstalled.en: node:22 bookworm base; Claude Code and Codex CLI (pinned), a TeX Live subset (ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS), python3 + uv, git, the shared controlled-search MCP server

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
